analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license to buy a gun, universal background checks, a waiting period, and an assault weapons ban.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; all 22 of its cosponsors were Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required everyone buying a gun or ammunition to first get a federal license — passing a background check, safety training, and a hands-on firing test — and renewed it every 10 years with fresh background checks. It would have extended background checks to nearly all gun transfers, added a 7-business-day waiting period, raised the purchase age to 21, closed domestic-violence loopholes for stalkers and dating partners, created federal 'red flag' court orders to temporarily remove guns from people deemed dangerous, banned assault weapons and silencers with federally funded buy-backs, banned untraceable ghost guns, imposed safety standards on gun locks and safes, raised federal gun taxes, repealed the industry's special protection from civil lawsuits, and funded community violence intervention and gun violence research. It was referred to three House committees and none of them ever acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: People and communities exposed to gun violence — particularly victims of domestic abuse, whose abusers could more easily be stripped of gun access under the bill's expanded definitions; families who could ask a federal court to temporarily remove guns from a relative in crisis; schools and college communities covered by expanded gun-free zones; police agencies receiving red-flag training grants; and community violence intervention groups receiving new funding.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal firearm owner's license: applicants must be 21, pass a written firearms-law test and hands-on firing test, submit to a background check and photograph, and renew every 10 years with an updated background check and annual re-screening.

Extends background checks to nearly all firearm transfers between private parties, with narrow exceptions for close-family gifts, loans at a shooting range or while hunting, and transfers by inheritance or in emergencies.
Replaces the 3-business-day default that lets a sale proceed if a check is unfinished with a mandatory 7-business-day waiting period before a transfer can be completed.
Closes loopholes in the domestic-violence prohibitions by covering dating partners, people protected by state or tribal domestic-violence laws, and people convicted of misdemeanor stalking.

Creates federal extreme risk protection orders that a family or household member or a law enforcement officer can seek in court — with no filing fee — to bar a person who poses a danger to themselves or others from buying or possessing guns, after a hearing and with firearms surrendered to a marshal's designee.

Bans new sales and possession of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, bans firearm silencers, bans untraceable and undetectable firearms, and funds buy-back programs through existing Byrne grants and a separate Justice Department buy-back program.

Raises the minimum age to buy any firearm or ammunition to 21, with exceptions for target practice, hunting, ranching and farm work, military duty, and inheritance of title, all generally requiring a parent or guardian's written consent.

Requires secure storage of guns where a minor or a person barred from owning guns could get them, with a $500 civil penalty per violation and up to 5 years' imprisonment if a minor or prohibited person actually obtains the gun.

Directs the Consumer Product Safety Commission — which is currently barred from regulating firearms — to set mandatory safety standards for gun locks and gun safes, and repeals the exclusion of pistols and revolvers from consumer product safety laws.
Repeals the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act shield, allowing victims to sue firearm manufacturers and dealers, and makes gun trace information usable in civil proceedings.

Raises federal excise taxes on firearms and requires gun dealers to keep sales records, undergo employee background checks and inspections, report lost and stolen guns, and comply with shop security requirements.

Authorizes grants for community violence intervention programs and for federal research on gun violence prevention, and funds state licensing systems, gun-dealer licensing, and red-flag law implementation.
Extends the federal gun-free school zones law to colleges and universities and removes the exception for people licensed to carry.

analysis.who_pays: Gun buyers and owners, who would face license costs, safety-training requirements, a waiting period, higher excise taxes, and storage and age restrictions; and the firearms industry — manufacturers and dealers — which would face an assault weapons and silencer ban, product safety regulation, mandatory inspections and record-keeping, buy-backs of grandfathered weapons, higher taxes, and lawsuits from victims now that its lawsuit shield is repealed.

drawbacks.text: The licensing regime adds real cost and delay for lawful buyers: applicants 21 and over must pass written and live-fire tests, undergo background checks and photography, and wait up to 40 days for a license before they can acquire a gun or even ammunition, and the 7-business-day waiting period further delays transfers — costs opponents argue fall hardest on people in rural areas far from training sites and on adults aged 18 to 20, who could no longer buy a long gun at all.

Secure-storage rules carry a $500 civil penalty per violation, escalate to as much as 5 years' imprisonment if a minor or a prohibited person obtains an improperly stored gun, and make improperly stored firearms subject to seizure and forfeiture — a real legal exposure for ordinary owners whose gun is taken in a burglary.

Because the bill restricts possession of a constitutionally protected item so broadly — universal licensing, an assault weapons ban covering grandfathered weapons, and a ban on possession of certain accessories — it would almost certainly face years of Second Amendment litigation, and the bill itself tries to short-circuit normal administrative review for the gun-lock rulemaking, which is a process objection even supporters of gun regulation would have to weigh.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large in scope: gun licensing, universal background checks, waiting periods, and red-flag laws are the measures most consistently associated in the research with lower gun deaths, and the bill attacks several channels — domestic violence, stalking, ghost guns, unsafe storage — at once. The costs are also real but mostly borne as friction by lawful buyers and as existential business risk by the industry, especially the combination of a licensing requirement, an assault weapons ban with buy-backs, and the repeal of the industry's lawsuit shield. Honest weighing has to note that the bill asked for everything at once, which is a serious design choice: it maximized the public-health case while making passage in a Republican-controlled House effectively impossible — which is exactly what happened.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to three House committees, then to a Judiciary subcommittee, it sat with no hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Hank Johnson (D-GA) introduced the bill on December 5, 2023.
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and also to Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce, the split reflecting provisions touching gun taxes, consumer product safety, and criminal law.
On December 8, 2023, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Health.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
All 22 cosponsors were Democrats; none was a Republican.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers and dealers, who avoided a federal licensing regime, an assault weapons and silencer ban with buy-backs, higher excise taxes, mandatory inspections and record retention, product safety regulation, and the repeal of their protection from civil lawsuits; individual owners also avoided new licensing, storage, and age requirements.

for.name: Rep. Henry C. 'Hank' Johnson Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Gun Violence Prevention and Community Safety Act of 2023 on December 5, 2023.

for.name: 22 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including members named in the introduction: Ms. Norton, Mr. Lynch, Mr. Quigley, Mr. Moulton, Ms. Lee of California, Mr. Goldman, Mr. Trone, Mr. McGovern, Mr. Espaillat, Mr. Keating, Mr. Auchincloss, Mrs. Napolitano, Mrs. Trahan, and Ms. Wilson, among others; every cosponsor was a Democrat.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of primary referral (118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup after the bill's referral; the record shows no committee action of any kind after the December 8, 2023 subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats and none was a Republican, and with a Republican House majority the bill never got a hearing or vote; no roll-call was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would end their fastest-growing product line with an assault weapons and large-capacity magazine ban plus buy-backs, ban silencer sales, classify semiautomatic assault weapons under the National Firearms Act, raise federal excise taxes, subject guns to Consumer Product Safety Commission rules for the first time, and repeal the law shielding them from most civil suits. The industry's interest in blocking the bill ran against the bill's public-safety aims, since nearly every provision restricted what the industry could sell.

Dealers would face a new license requirement to sell, employee background checks, mandatory record and inventory inspections, lost-and-stolen reporting, shop security rules, record retention after closing, and civil enforcement, while every retail sale would require verifying a customer's federal or state license through a new government database.

industries.industry: Gun industry civil-liability shield (repeal of the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act)
industries.note: The bill repeals the statute that has largely insulated manufacturers and sellers from lawsuits over criminal or negligent use of their products, opening the industry to civil litigation by shooting victims — the single biggest long-term legal exposure in the bill.

Mandatory consumer safety standards for gun locks and safes plus new secure-storage requirements create guaranteed demand for certified products; the industry's interest runs alongside the bill's child-safety and suicide-prevention goals.

industries.industry: Community violence intervention organizations and gun violence researchers
industries.note: The bill authorizes grant funding for community violence intervention programs and dedicated funding for research on gun violence prevention, fields that have historically been starved of federal support.
